rationale: A wins because it keeps the story lanes grounded and proof-gated, especially “The math behind Going's claim that paid members save $550 a flight.” B has real bones, but its flashiest angle, “The AI travel planner that books nothing,” rests on an unsourced premise: “AI agents that book everything” is not in the supplied update. A gives the founder pitchable material; B risks walking them into a reporter's first skeptical follow-up with borrowed context pretending to be fact.
gaps_in_A: “newsletter-born audiences get monetized as software” slightly imports a company-origin story beyond the supplied facts; the update gives the former name and member count, not the newsletter-to-software arc.
“live industry question about who owns the transaction” is plausible beat framing, but the supplied facts only prove Going links out and does not book in-app yet.
The set is strong, but it could state more bluntly that without paid-base size, usage data, or a demo, only the launch/category angle survives as a thin product brief.
gaps_in_B: “The prevailing belief, loudly marketed across the industry” is imported. A contrarian angle cannot stand on an industry narrative the update did not supply.
“it deliberately plans and links out” overstates intent. The facts say no booking happens in-app yet, not why Going made that choice.
“the deal that lands in your inbox” drifts from the given “app finds” framing and turns an alert fact into a channel claim.
“Next step: meanest-editor” is process recursion, not the founder's next useful move. The next step is proof collection, then journalist fit-check.
